title.value: Modelling and simulating organizational ransomware recovery: structure, methodology, and decisions
Applying staged event-driven access control to combat ransomware

authors.value: Ilau, M.-C.; Baldwin, A.; Caulfield, T.; Pym, D.

source_database.value: Google Scholar (lead) / verified against Oxford Academic publisher page (record indexed in Scopus/ScienceDirect-family sources via Oxford)

study_type.value: Simulation modelling study (compositional system-model construction with comparative simulation analysis)
System design with empirical prototype evaluation (access-control architecture + working OS-level prototype)

methodology.value: Semantically justified, mathematically compositional co-design system-modelling approach (process-algebra grounded): ransomware behaviour, organizational structure, IT infrastructure, and recovery options conceptualized from literature surveys and expert knowledge; model built as composition of four submodels (device, network, server, malware); compares endpoint device recovery mechanisms (including USB-stick OS-image recovery) over 9,000 parameter configurations totalling 450,000 iterations; results analysed in three organizationally relevant scenarios plus general-level sensitivity analysis

Staged Event-Driven Access Control (SEDAC) architecture combining program-centric access control (PCAC) and user-centric access control (UCAC), chained as three stages: pre-UCAC PCAC (OS integrity, MBR Guard), UCAC (user consent/intention), post-UCAC PCAC (user file integrity, File Warden minifilter) plus a Firewall Liaisor for exfiltration blocking; updated ransomware threat model covering novel attack vectors (fileless PowerShell-script encryption, 7-Zip-based encryption, VM-folder-mapped encryption, intermittent 25% partial encryption, unsafe MBR writes, outbound exfiltration) with redefined false positives/negatives; Sedaco prototype implemented on Windows 10 and evaluated against WannaCry/LockFile/Petya-class samples and simulations, compared with bare Windows 10, Windows Defender, two unnamed antivirus products, and the authors' earlier Fitico and Ranacco designs

key_findings.value: Demonstrates that a compositional simulation model can quantify the organizational consequences of recovery-solution choices (recovery time, cost, and resilience trade-offs) before deployment; situates the decision problem in empirical context (prior work reports 21% of 55 studied ransomware attacks fully disrupted business continuity for 2+ weeks and 19% needed months to recover, if at all); sensitivity analysis reveals which parameters most influence time-to-recover, supporting policy/technology mix decisions

The Sedaco prototype intercepted more types of ransomware attack vectors than existing proposals: File Warden blocked all directly initiated file-encryption activities (user-level PCAC); MBR Guard blocked all unsafe MBR modifications (OS-level PCAC); indirect encryptions (PowerShell/Command Line, VM-mapped folders) triggered UCAC user-permission warnings; Firewall Liaisor blocked outbound exfiltration the antivirus network firewall missed; the unnamed antivirus failed intermittent 25% partial encryption, unsafe random MBR writes, PowerShell/7-Zip/VM-based encryption, and outbound exfiltration - evidencing application-whitelist-only anti-ransomware logic

limitations.value: Model is only partially generic and parametrized from literature/expert judgement rather than validated against real recovered organizations; focus is endpoint device recovery rather than enterprise-wide (cloud, hypervisor, supply-chain) recovery; outcome realism depends on fidelity of the conceptualized ransomware/organizational behaviour

Prototype limited to Windows OS; UCAC inference of user intention/consent trades accuracy vs alarm fatigue, and human-presence heuristics can mis-fire; PCAC depends on software-industry cooperation on coding standards and file-type integrity enforcement that does not currently exist; explicit security-vs-usability dilemma for commercial adoption; user acceptance untested

research_gaps.value: Addresses the resilience-engineering gap: organizations lack evidence-based understanding of how backup/recovery mixes (technology + policy + employee factors) affect time-to-recover and cost; positions compositional modelling and sensitivity analysis as a decision-support instrument for ransomware resilience investment

Fills the gap of OS-native prevention: existing anti-ransomware studies ignore novel vectors (fileless scripts, partial encryption, exfiltration, human-operated ransomware); advocates embedding SEDAC-style access control into OS/architecture design and calls for research on non-negotiable vs user-delegable access decisions and usability perception
